before: The stored object may contain information a response should not reveal. Construct an explicit response rather than returning the whole stored row.
This exercise is a small pure JavaScript model. Its inputs are supplied directly; it does not receive live HTTP requests, operate a database, or deploy a service.
Reading note.id and note.title selects those values. The returned object has no ownerEmail or token field. Projection is separate from deciding who may read the note.

Read the function call publicNote({"id":1,"title":"Moon","ownerEmail":"private@example.test"}) from the inside out: the arguments supply the inputs, publicNote runs the body once, and return sends its result back to the caller. console.log displays that result; it does not change it.
A new private field is added to the stored row. What happens with this explicit projection? Only the named response fields are copied, so an unrelated stored field stays out.
after: A stored note may include private details that a response should leave out. Build the response by naming the fields it may contain, instead of returning the entire stored object.
This selection is called a projection. It decides what the response contains. A real server must also check who is allowed to read the note before sending it.
note.id and note.title read the two allowed values. The surrounding braces create a new object, leaving the stored note unchanged.
If another private field is added to the stored note later, this response still leaves it out. Only explicitly selected fields are copied. Copying every field would lose that protection.
Complete publicNote(note) with a new object containing only id and title. Keep those two values unchanged and leave all other fields out.
